headline: Make sound direction visible.
intro: SoundAround translates sound-direction estimates into peripheral LED cues. The wearable prototype explores how someone could locate a sound without checking a separate screen.
context: University of Michigan · Engineering Interactive Systems course project · Jan–Apr 2023
role: I originated the idea and handled hardware assembly, Python software, interaction design, testing, and results analysis. I did not lead the participant study sessions.

hero.alt: The original SoundAround helmet prototype with microphone array, Raspberry Pi, battery pack, and LED wiring, positioned in the five-direction study setup.
hero.caption: The working course prototype in the direction-identification setup. The numbered positions defined five front-direction targets.
hero.credit: Original course report, Figure 3 · Le Qin and Jeremy Zhengqi Huang

question.title: Can peripheral light communicate a sound's location?
question.text: Sound can originate outside the field of view. Motivated by accessibility for deaf and hard-of-hearing people, I explored visual cues that convey its direction while allowing the wearer to keep looking at their surroundings.

steps.title: Acquire direction
steps.text: Connect a ReSpeaker four-microphone array to a Raspberry Pi. The microphone device supplies direction estimates to a Python acquisition process.

steps.title: Map to peripheral light
steps.text: Share readings with a display process and map direction to LED position. Red and green distinguish front and rear sources.

steps.title: Refine from feedback
steps.text: Retune directional mappings, reduce brightness, add diffusion, and dim idle LEDs after preliminary feedback exposed interpretation and comfort issues.

gallery.alt: System diagram connecting a four-microphone array, Raspberry Pi 4, programmable LED strip, and portable power supply.
gallery.caption: Sensing, concurrent software, and wearable output form one system. The microphone supplies direction; the application makes it interpretable.

gallery.alt: Original interface sketch showing light position and color indicating front and rear sound directions around a wearer.
gallery.caption: The interaction sketch uses both LED position and color to distinguish where a sound originates.

finding.title: Interpretability mattered as much as sensing.
finding.text: The quiet-lab tasks showed that participants could interpret the cues. Outdoor tests exposed a different challenge: ambient noise could destabilize the indication and slow interpretation. That gap shaped the next questions about filtering and evaluation in everyday environments.

details: The reported percentages measure participant direction-identification tasks, not angular localization accuracy. Rear trials accepted pointing at or very near the target.
Noise-cancelling headphones limited auditory input; this condition does not reproduce or validate the deaf or hard-of-hearing experience.
The original source preserves experimental hardware/software variants. It documents the course prototype rather than a verified, reproducible product release.
credits: A collaboration with Jeremy Zhengqi Huang; we coauthored the course report.
Direction estimation came from the ReSpeaker device. My engineering connected its output to the wearable interaction and evaluation.
